-These experiments are now approaching a fundamental barrier.
-Standard Model neutrinos --- from the Sun, the atmosphere, and the diffuse supernova background --- also scatter coherently off nuclei, producing recoils that can mimic a dark matter signal almost perfectly~\cite{Cirelli:2024ssz}.
-This irreducible background, known as the \textbf{neutrino fog} (or neutrino floor), has qualitatively different consequences depending on the dark matter mass.
-Below ${\sim}\,10$~GeV, high-flux solar neutrinos generate recoil energies up to tens of keV that overlap with the expected WIMP signal.
-Above ${\sim}\,100$~GeV, lower-flux atmospheric neutrinos become the limiting factor~\cite{Cirelli:2024ssz}.
-Once an experiment's sensitivity enters the neutrino fog, the improvement in cross-section bounds slows dramatically --- scaling as the inverse square root of the exposure rather than inversely with it~\cite{OHare:2021utq}.
-The next generation of detectors, notably the DARWIN/XLZD program~\cite{DARWIN:2016hyl}, will reach multi-ton xenon exposures and begin to probe the neutrino fog directly.
-Pushing beyond this barrier may eventually require directional detectors capable of distinguishing the apparent ``dark matter wind'' coming from the Cygnus constellation from the isotropic neutrino background~\cite{Cirelli:2024ssz}.
currentVersionContext:
+Standard Model neutrinos --- solar, atmospheric, and from the diffuse supernova background --- scatter coherently off nuclei and produce recoils kinematically indistinguishable from a WIMP signal; this irreducible background is the \textbf{neutrino fog} (or neutrino floor).
+The question of whether it would ever actually show up in data was settled in 2021, when XENON1T recorded the first observation of solar $^8$B coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering (CE$\nu$NS) in a dark matter detector~\cite{XENON:2020gfr}.
+PandaX-4T and XENONnT have since reported independent indications at roughly $2.6\sigma$ and $2.7\sigma$, consistent with the expected solar rate~\cite{PandaX:2024muv,XENON:2024hup}; XENONnT also ran the first dedicated dark matter search inside the fog~\cite{XENON:2024hup}, and LZ set the world-best spin-independent WIMP bound while reporting its own $^8$B indications~\cite{LZ:2024zvo}.
+What this means practically is that the fog is already a feature of current data, not a future cliff: sensitivity gains slow from here, scaling as the inverse square root of accumulated exposure rather than inversely~\cite{OHare:2021utq}, and the next generation of detectors --- notably the DARWIN/XLZD program~\cite{DARWIN:2016hyl} --- will reach multi-ton xenon exposures designed to operate within the fog rather than to avoid it.
+Pushing substantially beyond it will likely require directional detectors capable of resolving the apparent ``dark matter wind'' from the Cygnus constellation against the isotropic neutrino background.

textPreview: We focus on WIMP--nucleus scattering as a methodological choice rather than as the full scope of direct detection, since other well-motivated candidates such as the axions introduced in Section~\ref{sec:1.2.1} require entirely different experimental strategies.

The standard probe is a resonant-cavity \emph{haloscope}: in a strong static magnetic field, an axion from the local galactic halo can convert into a microwave photon inside a high-quality-factor cavity tuned to the axion mass, producing a narrow excess above the thermal noise floor.
